newsitem.title: PERU: Japanese ambassador, former hostage, leaves Peru.
newsitem.headline: Japanese ambassador, former hostage, leaves Peru.

text.p: Japanese Ambassador Morihisa Aoki, one of 72 hostages rescued from Marxist rebels in a bloody raid at his residence, left Lima for Tokyo late on Saturday accompanied by his country's foreign minister, Yukihiko Ikeda.

Before boarding a Japan Airlines jet at 10 p.m. local time (0300 GMT), the silver-haired Aoki, 58, waved goodbye to Peru from a wheelchair, necessary because of a hip injury he sustained jumping through a window in the explosive escape on Tuesday.

Officials have not said if the ill-fated host of a Dec. 19 reception in honour of Japanese Emperor Akihito will keep his post as envoy to Peru. The diplomat has repeatedly apologised to his government because the reception he held turned into a four-month nightmare after 14 Tupac Amaru rebels stormed his home and took hundreds of his guests hostage.

Aoki's wife, Naok o Aoki, also boarded the plane. The couple had made an emotional return on Friday to the burned-out residence to retrieve the portrait photographs of their emperor and Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.
Ikeda, who accompanied them on a tour of the mined and booby-trapped residence, boarded the jet shortly after the couple and a 100-strong delegation of envoys and journalists.

The foreign minister, who completed a hectic three-day trip to thank the Peruvian government for Tuesday's rescue, was the last to board. He scurried across the runway and hurriedly bid farewell to Peru's acting foreign minister, Jorge Gonzales.

Gonzales is deputizing for Francisco Tudela, who is recovering in a hospital from bullet wounds sustained when commandos saved him and Aoki from the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) hostage-takers.

While Ikeda told President Alberto Fujimori that Tokyo was grateful the rescue had freed all 24 of the remaining Japanese captives, he also faulted Peru for failing to gather sufficient intelligence on the rebels to prevent their attack on the residence.
"Regarding the movements of the MRTA, if we had information, the crisis could never have happened," Ikeda told a news conference on Saturday.
His remarks were the first hint of an official rebuke from Tokyo and added to other criticism that has slowly dampened enthusiasm for Peru's spectacular rescue.

Praise from foreign governments poured into Peru immediately after the military's meticulously executed strike. But reports started to emerge later that commandos executed at least two captured rebels during the rescue.
If true, Tokyo could be acutely embarrassed by a flagrant violation of the Geneva Convention which took place in its residence -- technically on Japanese territory.

Fujimori did not warn Japan before he launched the rescue, which caught the rebels off guard playing soccer in a reception room. In a melee of explosives and gunfire, commandos burst out of tunnels dug under the mansion during the 18-week siege.
Fujimori vehemently denies the execution charges.

But a former hostage, a commando who took part in the raid, military, police and rebel sources said separately that troops shot to death two unarmed rebels they had caught and held in an upper-story room of the mansion.
All 14 of the Tupac Amaru rebels died in the attack, along with one hostage, a local judge, and two commandos.
Despite the execution accusations, Fujimori appeared determined on Friday to bask in the glory of Peru's most spectacular victory during its 18 years of guerrilla wars.

Buoyed by popularity ratings that soared after the rescue of the 71 VIPs, the president arranged a tour for Ikeda and a host of local and foreign journalists to show off the 3,000-year-old ruins of the Chavin de Huantar tunnels which he said gave him the idea for the ingenious raid.

"One early morning three months ago I woke suddenly and thought that if a peaceful solution was not possible, an option would be this kind of network of tunnels," Fujimori said after emerging from the ruins' underground labyrinth.

Sixty men, working 24 hours a day, spent three months and shifted 200 truckloads of earth to build a warren of tunnels underneath the diplomatic compound in Lima. Like Chavin de Huantar, the military's tunnels included sleeping and eating facilities, as well as food supplies.
